translations.text: During the plague the princes of Leinster came with their king, that is,
first to talk with Bran Ua Faeláin about what they should do against the plague that had come into the land of Leinster, that is,

whether each of them should go to his ancestral church to take the staff of [?] (bachall banaba) in one monastic city, that is, in the joint assembly of the kings, in whichever place they would choose [?].
Then Bran answered them and said to them: "This is what I recognise: we have been in disfavour with God until now in what we have been doing."
"What is right now is for us to be together for the rest of our lives, praying against the plague."
The princes then answered: "That is the choice of all of us." This is what he said to them
in their conversation, that is: "Let us go to Émíne Bán." Then they went.
They talked over with Émíne Bán what they had come for: to repent before God, to take the staff with him, and to work for the good of their souls for as long as they were alive.
Émíne answered them: "Let us all pray to God tonight that he may give us counsel about what you are discussing." Then they all stayed that night.
Then at daybreak Émíne called his community and said to them: "What shall we do about the trouble that has come to us?"
"If we turn them away after they have come, they will be angry. If they stay with us, it will grieve us if they die of this plague, since they have come to us for help."
Then his community answered Émíne: "Whatever you think best, we think best too."
"This, indeed, is my counsel, if you think it right:
let us beg the Lord to spare these men from the plague, and let an equal number of us go in their place, I myself in place of Bran."
"Yes, yes," his community said to Émíne. "We think that is right."
Then Émíne called the princes and said to them: "We have talked together, then," said Émíne,
"about you, and we have asked the Lord to help us protect you from this plague. This is how he has granted it:
the same number of my community as there are of you will go to heaven in your place, I myself in place of Bran."
Then the princes gave thanks to God and to Émíne, though Bran thought it too great a thing for Émíne to go in his
place. And all fifty princes around the king bowed down to the full will of glorious Émíne, whatever [?] he might impose on them.
Then Émíne said to them: "This is my demand: that you fear God and love him and amend your conduct toward God. Whoever does his favours for him is better than others [?]."
Then the princes said to Émíne: "What reward, then, will you have from us in return for the help given to us?"
"Shall we ourselves and our descendants be bound in service to you for ever as your church's tenants?" Émíne answered: "I will not take you as my tenants.
You have great sheep and a great fold of your own. This is a small fold with small sheep in it, but they are great in the will of God [?]."
"Tell us, then, what shall we give? Shall it be lands and estates, or treasures and wealth?" Émíne answered them:
[?] lest you should say [?]: it is a covenant that we have asked of God for you, concerning your being saved, [?] with abundance of wealth and land in return for it.
The question, then: is there anything else that we should give you?
There is indeed, said Émíne: your strength and support for this place, and its freedom forever, and the freedom of its land from anything [?]
that has been granted to it and released to it and offered to it; and whatever [?] concerning its disputes and its lawsuits, that they be dealt with along with the disputes of Leinster.
If its dispute is with the descendants of Bran, the will of the community itself shall prevail in that;

if it is with anyone else, the descendants of Bran and the sureties of Leinster in general are enforcers and judges for the full upholding [?] of the rights of Émíne Ain and his community against the Leinstermen.
Then Bran ua Fáeláin, together with the other rulers of Leinster, bound sureties for the full integrity of this freedom.
The other rulers bound it upon themselves and upon their descendants forever.
These are the sureties who were requested here and who came into the hand of Émíne Ain, namely:
Cellach son of Áed Crón, and Culdub son of Certán, Degchairdel son of Brocán, Fínán son of Máel Díbid, Ardmesach son of Máel Rois, Dub Cluana son of Furodrán, Eltíne son of Brocán, Buide son of
Laignén, Dub Dá Chrích son of Máel Ochtraig, Dímmusach son of Congal, Máel Tuile son of Máel Uidir, Áedán son of Eochu, and Fabnith ua Tusecháin, and Lapán and Mescell of Laois.
These, then, are the men we have listed, who were saved from the plague together with Bran; and it is to the ruler that the community goes;
it is he who summons the lords to them against any refusal, disturbance or violation of this freedom of Ros Glas.
This, then, was the arrangement Émíne made for offering up his community: these fifty around their king, namely:
seven each day until the end of a week, and Émíne himself last of all, in place of Bran, after singing the requiem of his community; and
Bran and his fifty warriors were to remain here until the end of the week, so that the fifty clerics who had gone in place of the fifty rulers might be shown to them,
and lots were cast among the fifty men of Émíne's community, so that each knew which group of seven would go in place of which others.
Then the group of seven from Émíne's community would go into one house with their monks to work [?]. The seven in whose place they were going
would dig graves for them [?] until they came afterwards; they would put on their eucharistic vestments,
they would go hand in hand, and Émíne would go before them to the rulers in whose place they were going, and would say:
Behold seven [?] of them here, whole, without sigh, without disease, and nothing else brings them except to go in your place.
The clerics would bid farewell to the laymen in whose place they were going, and each of them would put his arm around the other's neck.
The laymen would weep at this; the clerics, however, were joyful as they went to heaven.
Nevertheless, said Émíne, remember what you have promised me, so that you may have the help of God from heaven and of all our prayers.
It is right for you to remember my bell, which you have seen and heard laying my community to rest [?] in your place, [?] its being struck against you.
For on the day that you are cursed for your crimes, your life will be cut short.
There shall be no king or royal heir from the king, the prince or the young lord against whom this is done, and I do not commend [?] him to heaven, and there will be no prosperity
for them on earth either. And whoever else it is inflicted on, provided they are guilty, they shall have neither heaven nor earth.

This, then, is one thing he stipulated concerning the freedom of the church: whatever monk should take it, and whatever his kindred, provided he is accepted by the community, it is to be wholly free for Eimíne Bán, without disturbance and without alienation.
And no layman or laywoman is to be fed during the three Lents of the year, or on a Wednesday, or on a fast Friday, or on a Sunday, or after vespers,
or before terce. Let there be no serving [?], and let no bacon, meat or butter be given to a man of Leinster until Doomsday. This is under the guarantee of Eimíne Bán and on pain of his
curse together with all the saints and the righteous, and under the guarantee of these kings and princes, if these commands are not kept until Doomsday.
After that Eimíne remained for forty nights, singing the requiem for his community and restraining and regulating their affairs.
When the time came for him to go to heaven, he summoned Bran together with the nobles of Leinster to bid them farewell, and to show Bran that he was going to heaven
in his place, and that he would have lived to great age and old age had he not come into these plagues [?] in place of Bran.
Bran promised him whatever he would ask, [that] his chariot [?] [would go] to whichever of the Leinstermen he pleased [?]. But Eimíne asked only one thing of Bran then:
"That my cemetery be the burial place of a king," said Eimíne. "One of your descendants will come," said Eimíne,
"and his name will be Bran, and his tomb will be in my church, so that it may be an increase of freedom and honour for my community and my church among all the Leinstermen."
Eimíne received a blessing from the rulers and left another behind.
Then, without a sigh and without sickness, he went under protection to heaven, having secured the freedom of Ros Glas from the Leinstermen until Doomsday, etc.
